## Vocabulary

Terms this pack was harvested with, grouped by their relation to the concept; counts are units matched / sources. Zero-hit terms are listed under Coverage. On every unit line, `keywords:` names the terms that matched.

- **self**: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs (15/4)

## Structure and components

- [statement] The Parkinson's Foundation exercise page lists biking, running, Tai Chi, yoga, Pilates, dance, weight training, non-contact boxing and qi gong among exercise types that all have positive effects on PD symptoms; the APTA guideline says results across community-based exercise modes appear comparable for impairment and participation-based measures, suggesting no 1 mode is superior to another, while other comparisons favor 1 intervention over another and the essential components that distinguish more from less effective programs are not clear; a network meta-analysis of mind-body exercises (Bai et al.) concludes that superiority over other exercise modalities remains uncertain. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/exercise · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13751929/

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] In the Duncan and Earhart randomized trial, 62 participants were assigned to a twice-weekly community-based Argentine tango program or a no-intervention control group and assessed off anti-Parkinson medication; on the primary MDS-UPDRS-3 outcome the control group showed no significant change over 12 months whereas the tango group had a reduction of 28.7% (12.8 points), and the authors suggest that long-term participation in tango may modify progression of disability in PD. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21959675/ · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7406058/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] The APTA clinical practice guideline for physical therapist management of Parkinson disease states that physical therapists should recommend community-based exercise to reduce motor disease severity and improve nonmotor symptoms, functional outcomes, and quality of life, rating evidence strength as high and recommendation strength as strong. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11687919/
- [statement] In the Li et al. randomized trial (NCT00611481), 195 patients with Hoehn and Yahr stage 1 to 4 Parkinson's disease were assigned to tai chi, resistance training or stretching for 60-minute sessions twice weekly for 24 weeks, and the tai chi group performed better than the resistance-training and stretching groups on the primary outcome of maximum excursion (between-group differences of 5.55 and 11.98 percentage points) and on directional control (10.45 and 11.38 percentage points). (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3285459/ · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5618798/
- [statement] Meta-analytic findings on tai chi and qigong and quality of life in Parkinson's disease differ: Song et al. (15 RCTs) reported improved quality of life (ES=-0.393, p<.001), whereas a meta-analysis of seven systematic reviews (Fidan et al.) and a meta-analysis of thirteen RCTs of traditional Chinese exercises (Song et al., later version) reported no statistically significant quality-of-life effect. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5618798/ · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31116118/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12847013/
- [statement] Review authors state quality limits on the dance literature: an umbrella review of 55 systematic reviews rated the overall confidence in the results of 38 reviews (69%) as critically low; a systematic review of 20 RCTs (N = 723) reported that small samples and methodological limitations resulted in low-certainty evidence across outcomes; and a systematic review of sixteen RCTs noted that performance bias cannot be controlled because participants and personnel cannot be blinded to a dance intervention and that less than half of the studies used a low-risk randomization procedure. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11687919/ · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8456607/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7406058/
- [statement] Systematic reviews of boxing for Parkinson's disease differ: Wang et al. (13 studies, 402 patients, pre-post assessments of boxing interventions) conclude that boxing exercise can effectively improve both motor and non-motor symptoms with safety and high adherence, whereas Gonzalez-Devesa et al. (13 studies) report no significant pooled effect on functional mobility, balance, motor symptoms, gait and cardiorespiratory fitness and call the evidence uncertain, and Hernandez-Martinez et al. (eight studies, 100 older people) conclude that boxing does not significantly improve balance, cardiorespiratory fitness and health-related quality of life. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11983467/ · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11778260/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12179875/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6904341/
- [statement] Meta-analyses of yoga in Parkinson's disease report benefit with caveats about robustness: Ban et al. (ten studies, 359 participants) report better motor status (MD = −5.64) with yoga and state that their results should be interpreted with caution, Suárez-Iglesias et al. report that a meta-analysis on five RCTs found yoga more effective than passive control for motor symptoms, whereas a network meta-analysis of mind-body exercises (Bai et al.) found that the significant effects of yoga did not prove robust in sensitivity analysis. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8275425/ · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34533097/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13751929/
- [statement] Systematic reviews of Nordic walking in Parkinson's disease differ in how they characterize benefit: Salse-Batán et al. (twelve studies) report that none of the statistically significant benefits were clinically meaningful except for walking ability and that Nordic Walking does not lead to clinically significant changes in global motor impairment, functional mobility, balance and physical fitness, whereas De Santis and Kaplan (13 studies, 318 patients) report that symptom severity, walking speed and gait pattern consistently improved after 4 to 24 weeks of Nordic walking relative to baseline or any control condition during ON-phases of pharmacotherapy, while rating study quality as poor to moderate. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35593147/ · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32507150/

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] A meta-analysis of tai chi and qigong trials (Song et al.; 15 RCTs, 755 subjects) reported improvement in UPDRS III (ES=-0.444) and balance (ES=0.544), rated methodological bias low in 6 studies, moderate in 7 and high in 2, and noted that funnel plots suggested some degree of publication bias; a later meta-analysis of traditional Chinese exercises (thirteen RCTs, 859 patients) reported UPDRS-III MD -4.30 and Berg Balance Scale MD 2.63 versus usual control and noted that only one included study used a double-blind procedure. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5618798/ · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12847013/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] On dance and motor symptom severity the sources differ: the European Physiotherapy Guideline (first edition, December 2014) gives a weak recommendation against using dance to improve movement functions (UPDRS III), whereas two meta-analyses of randomized trials (Ismail et al., 20 RCTs; Carapellotti et al., sixteen RCTs) report better MDS-UPDRS scores with dance than in non-dancers or no-intervention controls. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinsonnet.nl/app/uploads/sites/3/2019/11/eu_guideline_parkinson_guideline_for_pt_s1.pdf · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8456607/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7406058/
- [statement] The European Physiotherapy Guideline (first edition, December 2014) gives a strong recommendation for using tai chi to improve movement functions (UPDRS III) and weak recommendations for using it to improve number of falls, balance capacity (BBS), walking speed, stride length, walking distance, functional mobility (TUG), muscle strength and functional reach, based on three CCTs in which 200 pwp participated. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinsonnet.nl/app/uploads/sites/3/2019/11/eu_guideline_parkinson_guideline_for_pt_s1.pdf · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs
- [statement] In a systematic review of sixteen RCTs involving 636 participants with mild to moderate PD, Carapellotti et al. reported that dance was favored over no intervention on MDS-UPDRS III (-2.31 points, p = 0.0004; four studies, n = 160) and balance (0.50 points, p = 0.0007; five studies, n = 206) but not on forward gait velocity (p = 0.44) or PDQ-39 (p = 0.65); an umbrella review of 55 systematic reviews (Pinto et al.) reported that dance added to usual care was better than usual care alone for motor symptoms severity, depressive symptoms, balance and functional mobility but not for gait distance and quality of life. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7406058/ · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11687919/
- [statement] Two randomized trials compared boxing with another active program: in Combs et al. (n = 31; 24-36 sessions of 90 minutes over 12 weeks) the traditional exercise group had significantly greater gains in balance confidence than the boxing group while only the boxing group showed significant improvements in gait velocity and endurance, and in Sangarapillai et al. (40 participants, 20-week trial) the sensory exercise group improved in comparison to the boxing group on a group-by-time interaction for the UPDRS-III (P = .036). (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23422464/ · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8414806/
- [statement] Adverse-event findings reported in the sources read: the APTA guideline reports that studies found no significant differences in adverse events between community-based exercise and the comparison groups, Li et al. observed no serious adverse events in their tai chi trial, and Ban et al. state that none of the included articles in their yoga meta-analysis reported serious adverse events. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3285459/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8275425/

## Research summary — Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs

Group-based exercise modes in Parkinson's disease are described by guidelines and reviews with mixed strength. The APTA guideline gives community-based exercise a strong recommendation with high evidence strength, while the European guideline gives only weak recommendations for dance and a strong one for tai chi on UPDRS III. Randomized trials report better limits-of-stability with tai chi than resistance training or stretching and better MDS-UPDRS-3 with 12 months of tango than no intervention. Meta-analyses diverge on quality of life for tai chi and qigong, on yoga robustness, on Nordic walking benefit and on boxing, and review authors describe dance evidence as low certainty or critically low confidence.

## Source disagreement — Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs

The APTA guideline cites its reference 174, the Combs et al. randomized trial, among studies indicating superior balance outcomes for boxing over traditional multi-modal exercise, whereas that trial's abstract reports that the traditional exercise group had significantly greater gains in balance confidence than the boxing group.

## Source disagreement — Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs

On dance and motor symptom severity, the European guideline gives a weak recommendation against dance for UPDRS III while two dance meta-analyses report better MDS-UPDRS III scores with dance than with no intervention.

## Source disagreement — Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs

Tai chi and qigong meta-analyses disagree on quality of life: Song et al. report an improvement while Fidan et al. and a later traditional Chinese exercise meta-analysis report no significant effect.

## Source disagreement — Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs

Boxing reviews disagree: Wang et al. report effective improvement of motor and non-motor symptoms while Gonzalez-Devesa et al. and Hernandez-Martinez et al. report no significant pooled effects.
